article_title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
citation: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6
title: Interactive-whiteboard CSCL toolset with shared visualization menus and collaborative argumentation annotations
description: A wireless interactive whiteboard (eBeam) with Bluetooth connects a server and three subgroup laptops on a local network, capturing traditional-whiteboard notes in real time into a meeting application visible on all laptops. Shared visualization tools provide "content specific menus" for patient history, vital signs, prescriptions, and decisions, structured like a hospital chart with vital signs placed centrally to highlight deterioration. Collaborative argumentation tools let observing students annotate, comment on, and suggest alternatives to the role-playing students' decisions, e.g. clinical suggestions like "listen to the lungs" or biomedical interpretations like "relevance of prednisone."
requirements: Networked laptops linked to the interactive whiteboard for each subgroup
Teacher documentation captured electronically in real time
target_learners: third-year medical students working in small groups
examples: Vital signs are put in the middle of the display to highlight the deteriorating situation, with decisions and prescriptions marked parallel to changing vital signs
key_sources: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6

article_title: The Effect of Interactive Whiteboard Applications Supported by Visual Materials on Middle School Students' Listening Comprehension and Persistence of Learning
citation: Abdulkadir Kırbas. (2018). The Effect of Interactive Whiteboard Applications Supported by Visual Materials on Middle School Students' Listening Comprehension and Persistence of Learning. Universal Journal of Educational Research 6(11): 2552-2561. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2018.061120
title: Use interactive whiteboards together with varied supporting materials and methods rather than alone
description: The article argues, from its constructivist-framed curriculum context, that interactive whiteboards by themselves are insufficient for achievement and persistence: "interactive whiteboards alone are inadequate to create the desired effect on academic achievement and persistence of learning". It recommends that boards be combined with diverse materials and other methods and techniques, as the experimental condition did by pairing whiteboard delivery with pictures, photographs and visual materials related to the listening text.
requirements: Interactive whiteboard use must be supported by a variety of materials and other methods and techniques
constraints: Stated for the Turkish course listening comprehension context under the constructivist-based 2018 Turkish Course Curriculum
target_learners: Middle school students in Turkish language courses
target_learning_goals: Listening comprehension and persistence of learning
examples: In the experiment, the same listening text was read aloud via interactive whiteboard applications while visual materials, appropriate pictures and photographs related to the text were shown to the experimental group
key_sources: Abdulkadir Kırbas. (2018). The Effect of Interactive Whiteboard Applications Supported by Visual Materials on Middle School Students' Listening Comprehension and Persistence of Learning. Universal Journal of Educational Research 6(11): 2552-2561. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2018.061120

article_title: Interactive Whiteboard for Primary Schools in Mauritius: An Effective Tool or Just Another Trend?
citation: Bahadur, G. K. & Oogarah, D. (2013). Interactive whiteboard for primary schools in Mauritius: An effective tool or just another trend? IJEDICT, 9(1), 19-35. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu//viewarticle.php?id=1559
title: Use the IWB for creative and interactive activities not possible with an ordinary whiteboard
description: The article concludes the IWB "is an essential teaching and learning tool when used appropriately" and "does not serve the purpose when teachers use it as an extension of the blackboard". It recommends that "Teachers should use IWBs for creative and interactive activities which would not be possible using an ordinary whiteboard", so the board's interactivity, multimedia and immediate feedback are exploited rather than replicated.
requirements: Teachers with sufficient ICT skills to prepare and run interactive activities
constraints: The IWB does not serve the purpose when used as an extension of the blackboard doing the same activities as an ordinary board
target_learners: Primary school pupils and teachers in Mauritius
examples: Pupils dragged words into boxes that would not accept a wrong answer, and clicked objects on the board to reveal more information
key_sources: Bahadur, G. K. & Oogarah, D. (2013). Interactive whiteboard for primary schools in Mauritius: An effective tool or just another trend? IJEDICT, 9(1), 19-35. http://ijedict.dec.uwi.edu//viewarticle.php?id=1559

article_title: Efficacy of Interactive Whiteboard on Psychomotor Skills Achievement of Students in Isometric and Orthographic Projection
citation: Gambari, I. A., Balogun, S. A., & Alfa, A. S. (2014). Efficacy of Interactive Whiteboard on Psychomotor Skills Achievement of Students in Isometric and Orthographic Projection. Contemporary Educational Technology, 5(4), 316-330. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1124320
title: Interactive whiteboard as a multi-stimulus presentation technology supporting diverse learning types
description: The article frames the interactive whiteboard as "a technology that transmits computer screen to the whiteboard by means of a projector and that enables controlling the computer by only touching the whiteboard with a special pen." Drawing on Wood et al. (2008), the authors explain IWB effectiveness through its capacity to diversify representation: "IWB diversifies the system of representation through the use of various stimuli (images, sounds and movement) and address the needs of diverse types of learning (visual, psychomotor, and affective)." This account explains the achievement advantage found in the study.
requirements: Availability of the IWB hardware, projector, and web-based resources in classrooms
constraints: Few rigorous studies exist on IWB impact on learning; conflicting evidence includes negligible effects reported by Higgins et al. (2007) and lower scores reported by Christophy and Wattson (2007)
examples: The teacher presented information and displayed animation of contents in 3-dimensional view to learners using IWB across eight sub-units
key_sources: Gambari, I. A., Balogun, S. A., & Alfa, A. S. (2014). Efficacy of Interactive Whiteboard on Psychomotor Skills Achievement of Students in Isometric and Orthographic Projection. Contemporary Educational Technology, 5(4), 316-330. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105500

article_title: Application of integrated whole-course clinical learning combined with case-based learning in undergraduate otolaryngology clerkships.
citation: Su Xiaoqun, Hu Bing, Liu Chengcheng, Ren Hongmiao. (2026). Application of integrated whole-course clinical learning combined with case-based learning in undergraduate otolaryngology clerkships. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09871-8
title: Integrated whole-course clinical learning (IWCL): following a patient across the full care continuum
description: IWCL is described as "a comprehensive, practice-oriented educational approach designed to expose undergraduate students to the full trajectory of patient care." Students follow selected patients from outpatient consultation through inpatient management to the surgical stage, connecting every stage of the clinical process. The model emphasizes "integrative learning, clinical thinking, and reflective practice," aiming to move students from fragmented observation to holistic patient-centered competence. In this study it was combined with case-based learning for an otolaryngology clerkship.
requirements: Requires supervising physicians to screen suitable surgical patients and closely monitor and guide the entire process, at associate chief physician level or above
constraints: Limited number of suitable surgical patients eligible and willing to be admitted; implementation places high demands on supervising physicians' time and energy
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in clinical clerkships
target_learning_goals: Specialty physical examination and documentation skills
examples: In the study, IC group students followed patients through outpatient consultation, inpatient management including admission note preparation, and surgical stages with preoperative planning and postoperative review.
key_sources: Su Xiaoqun, Hu Bing, Liu Chengcheng, Ren Hongmiao. (2026). Application of integrated whole-course clinical learning combined with case-based learning in undergraduate otolaryngology clerkships. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09871-8

article_title: Application of integrated whole-course clinical learning combined with case-based learning in undergraduate otolaryngology clerkships.
citation: Su Xiaoqun, Hu Bing, Liu Chengcheng, Ren Hongmiao. (2026). Application of integrated whole-course clinical learning combined with case-based learning in undergraduate otolaryngology clerkships. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09871-8
title: Combining a whole-course clinical trajectory with case-based learning in a specialty clerkship
description: The article's combined teaching model builds on CBL by adding IWCL, "emphasizing case analysis, interactive participation, and continuous clinical engagement." The clerkship curriculum integrates theoretical review, specialty physical examinations, outpatient shadowing, anatomical study, and admission note writing, with different teaching methods matched to each subject's characteristics. The design aims to maximize students' subjective initiative and connect theoretical knowledge to clinical practice.
requirements: Different teaching methods must be integrated across curriculum subjects; supervising surgeons provide explicit guidance and discussion on imaging, surgical indications, and surgical plans
constraints: Evaluated in a single institutional otolaryngology clerkship setting; group-level allocation with preexisting clerkship groups limited concealment and blinding
target_learners: Fifth-year undergraduate medical students on clinical clerkships
target_learning_goals: Integration of theoretical knowledge and practical clinical skills
Clinical thinking and specialty competence in otolaryngology
examples: The IC group received IWCL combined with CBL while the LC group received CBL combined with LBL, with outcomes compared across examination scores, proficiency scales, and satisfaction.
key_sources: Su Xiaoqun, Hu Bing, Liu Chengcheng, Ren Hongmiao. (2026). Application of integrated whole-course clinical learning combined with case-based learning in undergraduate otolaryngology clerkships. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09871-8
